newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-New Australian trade report off to good start.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-New Australian trade report off to good start.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Statistics' newest monthly report, the international balance on trade of goods and services, got off to a better than expected start on Monday with a deficit at the low end of expectations.
The January deficit came in at A$63 million, well under the median forecast of a A$230 million deficit.
Forecasts had ranged from a flat result to a deficit of A$500 million, although there was only one forecast for the deficit to be under A$100 million.
The trade and services balance report has replaced the monthly current account deficit report.
"It's pleasing to see it lower than expectations, with imports and exports roughly in balance," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
The January deficit represented a turnaround of almost A$300 million from the December surplus of A$235 million.
Within the overall deficit, trade of goods was in deficit by A$255 million, while services posted a surplus of A$192 million.
"One of the interesting points was that the exports side appears to have held up very, very well in that month," Axiom Funds Management economist Matthew Drennan said.
"We had a very big rise in December and it seems to have held those levels right through in January, so that's encouraging," Drennan said.
Exports of goods were up 0.2 percent in Janaury after their strong 7.4 percent rise in December.
After data showing a 5.7 percent rise in Janaury imports was released last month, it was primarily expected that weakness in exports that was behind the forecasts of a larger deficit.

The data was also affected by substantial net credit revisions, totalling A$5.2 billion since the 1985/86 (July/June) fiscal year. For the six months to December, the net trade balance was improved by A$483 million.
While the January trade deficit was lower than expected, most economists see the overall current account deficit as being on a widening trend on the back of a strengthening economy through 1997.
"It's not unduly high at a time when the economy is reasonably soft, and so we can expect that to widen as the year progresses," said Rothschild Australia economist Ric Simes.
The monthly current account deficit was replaced because the income components were extrapolations of quarterly data and were subject to often large and constant revision.

To imporve accuracy and reliability of the data the Australian Bureau Statistics decided to publish only trade details monthly, with the income components being reported in the quarterly balance of payments.
